note.text: Consonants can be compared by place, manner and voicing. Lip closure produces the stops /p/ and /b/; /b/ is voiced and /p/ voiceless. The initial sounds /t/ and /d/ are alveolar stops. The pairs /f/ and /v/, and /s/ and /z/, are fricatives: air passes through a narrow opening rather than being fully stopped. Letters and sounds are different systems. This lesson covers selected contrasts, not the full inventory. Written choices do not assess hearing, accent or spoken production.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify selected consonant contrasts and explain voicing and manner. Builds on: word forms, listening scripts and clause structure. Leads to: editing written speech and teacher-led pronunciation practice.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original pairs: pin/bin, tie/die, fan/van and sip/zip. Each changes an initial consonant while keeping the rest comparable. /p/ and /b/ use the lips; /f/ and /v/ involve lower lip and upper teeth. A teacher can model these words aloud and check recognition and production.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify the requested words, compare place and manner, then identify the voiced member. Use a teacher’s spoken model for actual listening and pronunciation practice. A correct written label does not demonstrate accurate pronunciation.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Every different letter marks only a voicing contrast. Correction: Letters do not automatically specify one articulatory difference.
/p/ and /b/ need lower-lip contact with upper teeth. Correction: That describes the labiodental model, not bilabial closure.
/t/ and /d/ begin fan and van. Correction: Fan and van begin with /f/ and /v/.
Every fricative requires complete stop closure. Correction: Friction and complete stop closure are different manners.
